ST. THOMAS, FEBRUARY 12, 1840. Our latest dates received bv the Packet from Copenhagen go to the 20th of December. The town remained tranquil, and no new measures of a general importance bad as ye taken place, though it was generally announ. ced that changes were at hand, and that the .machinery of Stale would receive renewed impulses, by the desire of His Majesty for reforms and improvements. The finances of the country were to bo taken in immediate consideration. The deceased King was laid out in State in his palace, and the Public had been admitted since the 18th December to see the body which has been dressed in the robes of corn nation, arid the crown, emblems of state and different orders ot Knighthood arranged round the open coffin The body is embalmed and the features not in the least altered. It is |jl represented as a most melanch dy and solemn Bj spectacle: the staircases and sal ions are covered and hung in black, dim lamps aie miming day and night, and thousands are thronging to see the venerable features of the deceased Monarch. 'The corps would be removed from Copenhagen on the 15th oj- January, when a magnificent funeral prunes. «ion wouid be formed at night bv torch lights þÿ and the coffin finally deposited in the royai vaults in the Cathedral of Roeskilde King Christian has received congratulatory addresses and deputations from all the different parts of the country, expressing at he same time with much frankness the wishes hopes ami expectations of the people We give a few of those, which seem most inter-

esting. The Royal Society of Sciences sent on the fi.h a deputation to His Majesty, as their former president. The Secretary of the Society, the celebrated Professor H þÿ( Dcisted . after having expressed the hope <! the scientific part of the country, to he furthermore protected under the reign of the King, concluded his address as follows: þÿ þÿ We would not be justified in this unfeigned joy, with which we present our congratulations, if we built our hope on your Majesty, merely as the friend and protector of the sciences. If we had taken such a narrow view, it might justly he thought, that we had not comprehended the intimate and manifold connexions between the sciences and the actual life. No we are aware, that your Majesty will not exclusively be the King and Protector of the mail of sci. ences or arts, or the military man, or any other separate class of citizens ; but that you comprehend and embrace all the different relations of life with the same care We live in a great and remarkable age, full of dangers, impending dangers, as well to the people, as to i he Piinces. In the course of centuries new powers have been unfolded, they have multiplied in all possible directions, and threaten to burst violently through . the old forms unless wise and peaceable reforms prevent such civil commotions, whose end, if they should overpower us. perhaps no one now alive night be allowed to see. The recollection, that vour Majesty has also taken your part in this cultivation of our times, and that you have al-

ready more than once proved to understand its character and necessities, is a thought which inspires us with confidence. We built our hope, not only on the knowledge of btisi' ness, the zeal for a lively and well organized prngess, the capacity to give motion to all the

different members, composing the State machinery, of which the Heir to the Throne so frequently gave proofs ; but we rejoice, that your Majesty will carry with you on the throne the enlightened and liberal ideas of our time and a full knowledge of the world, obtained in the school of experience. Your Majesty would undoubtedly not think, that we expect sudden and crushing reforms; on the contrary, we entertain a hope, that those great and manifold improvements, which have become necessary by the lively progress of our times, may at once he taken up with vigour and conducted with a wise circumspection, under the guidance of your Majesty, to whose mind ii resolute vacillation was always foreign- Standing before your Majesty in tins solemn moment, 1 thought it my duty to pronounce the confident hope of the people, not as anything mw. not as a matter with which your Majesty had not been acquainted, hut the patriot must express the wants and feelings of the country, and the State is imbued with new file, when the King feels convinced, that his great and good intentions ate rooted in the heat is of his people, and the love of the people receives tresh nourishment through the conviction of the power, ability and good wilj of the King. In our times the words spoken in the palaces of Princes resound to the most distant cottages, and I earnestly hope that may have contributed my mite, to revive and nourish that intimate relation between the People and the King, which from old times

was natural to the Danish Nation. We pray, that the Almtghty will send his assistance and his rich blessings over your Majesty, and our beloved Country, which you have been called to govern þÿ On the day alter the old þÿKing s death a Deputation of Students at the University of Copenhagen delivered the following Address to His Majesty : þÿ þÿ Most Gracious Ivi -g! We the undersigned vour þÿMajesty faithful s subjects, Academic citizens ol the University of Copenha gen. have with the most lively sensation received the giave notice of your Majesty having ascended the throne of your forefathers. We bring your Majesty our most respectful congratulaiiou on this important occasion, when the welfare of a whole nation has been laid in your hands. With, a clear insight and a lively desire for every thing good and noble, your Majesty have faithfully cultivated and protected the sciences and Arts. No wonder then, if the young Student should befound foremost amongst those, who w;th joyful ex pectalions salute the new reign, which promises Denmark, under the enlightened care of your Majesty, a fruitful and lively devclope ment of all the higher benefits of life. The liberty of the press is one of the most essen tial conditions for giving life to the most exalted interests of human mind, it is the trios powerful support to the virtue, liberty and education of Nations. The enlightened and liberal mind of your Majesty we hold as a guarantee, that t lie press will be liberated from

those restrictions, by which it has hitherto been encumbered. 'This character of your Majesty makes us confident, that you will protect with a strong arm a free developement of all good and useful powers, and a free organization of the relations between the State and the People, on which all mental and so. cial progress is dependiug. We do not leoi confident of possessing a dear insight in all matters of state ; but this we know, that a powerful regeneration is required, if our he loved country after having been visited by a

suecesion of the most grave misfortunes, shn 1 ever regain that honour, liberty and prospeii t v, which are justly claimed by the nation ant due to an enlightened people, whose faithft. character and love of order has been repeat edly tested. We rejoice in that conviction that vour Majesty, a son of these new times, have understood its claims, that vou rom< prepared to this great work of regeneration, whose successful termination will give add i tional lustre and blessings to your name, bv extensive studies, by a thorough knowledge of the institutions of foreign countries, and bv the experience redacted from your intercourse with the most enlightened men of our age The world has long ago had an unfailing proof of the spirit which is to animate your Majesty s reign ; you have given a beloved brothernation, whose mental cultivation was certainlv not superior to I hat of the Danish people, a Constitution, giving fife to dornant powers, and preparing in the annals of history those honours, which your Majesty may now con firm in the most splendid way. The Prede cessor of your Majesty, by carefully attending to the education of the People, whilst introdu cing representative forms, led the country oik momentous step on towards t ho necessities o our enlightened times. Denmark and the whole civilised world, have turned their eves, w ith confidence and expectation, on the crea tor of the celebrated Norwegian Constitution, hoping that all this may he fulfilled to the hen our and rejoiceing of your Majesty, and fin

the salvation and blessing of vour People The external relations, which influence, ainl ei t her check or give impulse to the progress of the mind, having thus come in harmony will the demands of the times and the cultivation of the people, the revived national spirit w il, unfold such riches nnd beauties, as would con stitute your þÿMajesty reign s one of the most prosperous and honoured epochs of the Danish history. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, February 1, 1840. BY THE PATRICK HENRY. Yesterday afternoon wo published a second edition, containing the most interesting intelligence brought by the packet-ship Patrick Henry þÿ this we republish to day on our first page, and add below farther summaries from the London and Liverpool papers The London Times says that the Queen's marriage will take place on the 4th of February þÿ Tuesday next. The papers abound with announcements of what is to bit done on the grand occasion þÿ for example, that gold Ittufi boxes will be given to all the foreign I þÿambassadors qucrr, the connexion between snuff and matrimony ? þÿ that the crown jewels are to be reset, &c. Lord Paimerslon and the Dowager Countess Cowper were married on the IHth of December. The lady is sister to Lord AJeibourne, and in her 53d year. Loid Palmerston is in his 50th. The United Service Gazette says that the Queen's marriage will be signalized, among other things, by a revival of a female order of knighthood þÿ or rather of that branch of the order of the garter winch was established by Richard 11., and included the ladies of the knights. The report is again circulated in the papers, that Lord i'oasonby is to be succeeded >y the Earl of Durham, as ambassador at Constantinople þÿ and as usual, the change is ascribed to the influence of Russia. I.ord Auckland has been elevated to an Earldom, with the same title. Sir John Keane has been made Lord Keane þÿ Mr. Mc'Naghten and Col. Pottiuger, baronets. þÿ It is reported that Lord Normanby is to be

appointed Governor General of India, as sue : ssor to Lord Auckland. It is rep >rt"d that Mr. O'Connell intends to resign his sat in Parliament. If the report is true, his otiject can oulv be to devote himself exclusively to the work of agitation The accounts from the in aaut iciiiriug districts are extremely unfavourable, and there can be no doubt that severe <1 stress exists, and is likely to exist, among the operators and the peasantry. The inferior quality of English grain kept down the prices, and of course kept up the duties þÿ the consequence was that the flour shipped from this country remained in bond, but little oi it having found us way into lite market. From the Bunker's Circular. We have good ground for staling that the bullion in the Bank at this instant considerably exceeds £3,500,(100. The amount of silver e ported since the 4th of December, to Hamburg chiefly þÿ reaching above £200,000 in þÿvalue is for the regulation of the exchange, and the highest authorities in the city on this matter express gieat confidence that the exchanges will be set to right without renewed diificulty and alarm. The unfavorable quotations of the lust three post days would not give a correct impression of their state, for it is known that by resorting to drawing bills even to the amount of a sum less than £ 10,000, the exchange with Hamburg would have been kept at its former level. There is, we believe, no amount ol bills now being drawn on the continent on London for the purpose of being
discounted in our rnon :y market, and the proceeds sent out in bullion.

FRANCE. a PARIS, Dec, 28. The Tartare steamer arrived in Toulon on the 124th instant, with dispatches from Algiers oi the 21st. The Moniteur Algerien of this date contains the following report Algiers, Dec. 20. " The moveable column under the orders of Gen. Rulricres, succeeded on the 14lh ami 15th in overtaking the Arabs, who overran the territory adjoining Belidah. Two engagements, very honorable for our troops, in which the enemy sustained a considerable loss. " The first encounter occurred in advance of Mered. The moveable column, on its way to Belidah with a convoy, perceived the enemy at a short distance ot tire embranchment of the two roads leading to the upper and lower camps. A battalion of Abdel Kader s regular infantry, having attempted to lake a position in Ironi of our troops, was vigorously attacked by them, cut to pieces b_, die Chasseurs, and driven in disorder into a ravine, pursued bv the French þÿInfantry. Between 50 and tiO dead Arabs remained on die field, and we bad five killed and 20 wounded. During the ali'air 300 Arabian horsemen, having made a movement to turn the convoy, were charged by 100 Chasseurs, and put to flight with the loss of 12 men killed and several horses. "In the morning of the 15th, while the convoy was entering the citv of Belidnh, Gen. iiudrieres advanced with part of ins troops and artillery, between the town and the Chifl'a, on the right bank of die Oundel Ivcbir. The Arabs having shown themselves in large numbers on the opposite side, a livelv fusillade

commenced, and the 2d Regiment of Light Infantry having crossed the liver, destroyed a detachment of the enemy which had descended from the mountains. They must have suffered considerable loss; 14 of their dead remained in our power. We had on our side 5 killed and 01 wounded. " The steamer which arrived to day from Phillippeville, announces that every thing was tranquil in the province of Consiantiue, where no acts of hostility had yet been committed bv the natives. The sanatory condition of the troops was improving. The construction of hospitals and barracks was proceeding with activity, and the Kabyh's had supplied a number of operatives to assist the engineers in raising - those buildings. O " A merchant vessel just arrived from Oran brought intelligence of the commencement of hostilities in that quarter. An engagement had already taken place bevond Mostaganem between the natives in the pay of France and the Arabs of Abdel Kader, the particulars of which were not yet known. " The 58th Regiment of the line, a portion of the 3d Light Infantry, and numerous detachment of soldiers belonging to the dilli;rcnt corps of the division have arrived from France."

RUSSIAN DECLARATION OF WAI AGAINST CHI VA. The 'Prussian State Gazette of the 20th instant, under head of St. Petersburgh, Dec 11, publishes a declaration of war of the Russian government, explaining the motives of a military expedition ordered against the Khai ot Chiva, an Asiatic province, situated in the west, on the Caspian Sea, and extending oi the south to Persia. 7'he object of this expedition, which is commanded by Lieut. From the London Spectator, Get. 10. The buoyant appearance of the Money Market to which we last week alluded has given place to one of a very different character, and ils aspect has been as gloomy during the present as it was lively duiing the past week. The change is, we believe, chiefly attributable to the financial operations of the Bank of the United States. It will be in the recollection of our readers, that large remittances in bullion were expected by the two recent arrivals of the great Western and British Queen steam vessels from New York; and although the amount actually received was about £256.000, it was less than had 1 been anticipated. A large remittance in Bonds was, however, received, and an arrangement has been concluded, by which these assets have been made available. A loan to the extent of £800.000 has been contract d by Mr. Jaudon on the behalf ot tiie United States Bank, to bear interest at the rate ol 6 per cent per annum, redeemable at par in the years 1841 and 1842. The pi ice at which it lias been taken is 92. The dividends are payable at Messrs. Denison Ai þÿCo. s,Lombard st. with whom are deposited, as collateral security, the same amount (£800.000) of Philadelphia State Bonds. It is now at from 3 to 4 per cent premium. This arrangement has materially increased the demand lor money, and the prices of almost every description of English security have declined from to f per cent. t It is stated, that the Bank Directors are very earnest in pressing the Government to

issue an order in council for suspending in their favor the act of Parliament by which the circulation of notes for sums of less than £5 is prohibited. The Ministry are, however, understood to have refused compliance with this request. The usual monthly statement ol the liabilities of the Bank will be puolished to-morrow ; and it is generally be lioved, that the amount of bullion in store will not be augmented, as. though there have been some large importations, the necessity 1 of paying the small dividends in rash lias abstracted 700,000 sovereigns from the Bank coffers ; but, as this bullion has not been re ported, a considerable part of it must soon find its wav back again. The foreign exchanges have declined slightly, and the appearance of them is heavy. It is understood that the Bank has drawn upon Paris to the full extent of the amount (£1000,000.) that the Bunk of France undertook to discount; and, as this support to the exchanges has been withdrawn, a further decline is anticipated. " þÿ a n SH ALL I GET M ABIDED ? OB, THE FINAL BESULVE j OF A BAOHELOB. S þÿ Rather than bear those ills I hare, þÿI fly ll to others which I know not þÿof.

Shall 1 get married ? said I to myself three times ere I had finished my second cup of bohea. Of late, indeed this pleasing question I she quarrels with all, and all has often suggested itself to me ; and the more frequent the suggestion, the firmer doth my resolution, in the affirmative, become. The perpetual toil, anxiety of mind, and petty I hood, for more than a circuit of, at least, a

disappointments to which 1 seem doomed require one grand struggle for emancipation. Shall I get married, and thus end þÿ em all ? En verite, 1 shall do so the very first opportunity. Let but one offer be made ; let but one nymph, young, old, or middle-aged, be hall as willing as I am literally compelled to be, and l am her own. No matter what her beauty, accomplishments or fortune be, I cannot change but for the better ; let her squint, be pug-nosed, toothless, or have a " huge mountain on her back." it will signify very little to the great question of happiness involved in my present dolorous situation. I'ew pity the miseries of an old bachelor. But. listen, ye callous of heart, and ye, vet unfledged, uninitiated striplings, hearken unto the words of experience. þÿ It you have tearsf prepare to shed them þÿnow, ye kind-hearted maidens, of all ages, sizes, complexions, and dispositions. From mv youth upwards, until a few years ago, I was the sport of capricious and cruel fortune in undergoing all the vicissitudes ot a lodger. Thcie is not one street in , ol the age of a respectable barrister, namely, five þÿyears standing, in which I have not domiciled. In many 1 have been living, some time or other in every angle, side, and cranny of the locality, until I have become literally acquainted with the very buildings? in others short was mv sojourn. In lact, 1 have outstripped all my contemporaries in this kind of migrative experience 1 have lodged with families of from twelve to

a couple : from a colony of children to a couple of sexagenarians. I have been robbed, swindled, traduced, imposed upon, and decried ; cajoled, plundered, privately and publicly, times without number ; my books and wardrobe taken, in one place, by distraint for the landlady's rent ; in another, ball burnt to death by fire through carelessness. In one house, the landlady would have me marry her daughter, voteus nolens ; 111 another, the landlady herself became willing to make me a Benedict. The perceptive organs are well developed ; order is particularly full, hut number is moderate ; and stranger still, the position of the eyes affords no indication of any remarkable fulness of language. Beaiti'es of the Thames þÿ From Chiswick upwards there is a constant succession of beautiful villas, only to look at which is enough satisfy to the traveller that he is indeed in England. Such neatness, such cleanliness, such variety of flower and tree peeping

ivy covered walls, and such comfort visibly dwelling over all, meet the gaze of the passer by no where but in England. We have sailed up other rivers in our time, have seen the castles of the Rhine, the chateaux of the Seine, and the villas of the Elbe, the Scheldt and the Meuse ; but never have we met with scenes of such elegant luxury as all England is dotted with. There is more appreciation of the simple loveliness of nature in England than in any other country in the world ; even our poorest cols embellish their poverty, and render it more endurable by nicely trimmed gardens both in the front and rear. Flowers and trees are the poor þÿman l s uxuries in England. The gew gaws of the art are beyond his reach ; but roses and lilies, violets, blue bells, and anemones, and all the tribes whose very names are pleasant, adorn his humble windows, and show the taste of the indweller, as well as the rich vases, golden time-pieces or choice paintings, that solicit our admiration in the chambers of the rich. How different is it in most of the countries on the Continent, especially in Germany, France and Belgium ! There, neither rich nor poor have that love for verdure and flowers which is so characteristic of ail classes of Englishmen. Their rivers show no such embowered villas and cottages on their banks as ours ; the country houses of their gentry are naked and ta steless in comparison, and their cottages are miserable huts, around whose doors or windows the honey suckle never crept, and even a flower

Bristol, Oct. 14. þÿ The merchants of Bristol, who have been, since the opening of the trade, the largest importers of tea in the kingdom, with the single exception of the port of London, have drawn up a memorial to Lord Palmerston upon the subject of the present state of the trade with China, which it is intended to present to his lordship during the present week. The memorialists state, that from the opening of the trade in 1834, they have imported 10 cargoes of tea to Bristol in British bottoms, comprising a freight of 12,000 tons and producing a revenue to the country of about £1,000,000 sterling; that they have not been in any manner connected with the opium trade. The memorialists then go on to complain, that while superintendents, &c., have been appointed bv this country, which fiave cost the country upwards of £100,000, yet they do not appear to have possessed any power either to restrain the unruly amongst her þÿMajesty subjects s in China, or to protect the injured from the aggressions of their fellow-countrymen, or of the Chinese, not possessing, in fact, even the power of police magistrates in England in cases of felony and misdemeanor, nor of insuring British subjects and British property from the cruelty, arbitrary imposition, or plunder of the Chinese government. The memorialists next complain, that although Lord Palmerston has twice or thrice introduced a bill to the House of Commons to form courts of civil and criminal judicature and a Court of Admirably

in China, yet six years have now passed, during which more than 3000 British subjects have annually visited China, and have been living at Canton, Whampoa, &c., or have been engaged in smuggling opium on the coast of China, unrestrained by the laws of their country. The memorialists next refer to the fact of the tea trade, which has þÿbro t a revenue to this country of £3,300,000 sterling per annum, having been continually placed in jeopardy by the smuggling trade carried on upon the coast, as well as by the pertinacious, corrupt, and overhearing conduct of the Canton local government, that the tea trade has also been especially jeopardised during the hist three years by the numerous ships employed upon the coast of China in smuggling opium, and more seriously injured by the intrusion of various þÿseh rsand small craft into the Canton river, the owners and crews of which have loo frequently set all laws, obedience, and authority at defiance, in consequence of which much bloodshed and violence have taken place on the river. The memorialists then charge the government with having sanctioned the smuggling of opium

The following received by the late arrival from Europe will attract the attention of capitalists. It is from responsible authority. American Stocks. þÿ The late loan made by the U S. Hank for about two years, and for £800,000 on deposit of Pennsylvania and other States, stock, at a price which gives 10 per cent, annual interest to the subscribers, shews what rate of interest must be paid to obtain any amount of money on the best American securities and serves therefore as a guide to capitalists here for their purchases of State stocks. We quote the last prices of the principal securities at which business has been done, but must add, that even at these rates, only small and occasional sales are practicable. The continued fall in their value destroys speculation, whilst many years will be required for real investments to absorb all that is at present in our market. We do not doubt, but that such gradual purchases will continue of the stocks of well known states which do not over issue, and which faithfully meet their engagements to their creditors, as the confidence in the resources of national Oonor ol the (J. States remains undiminished in this country, as well as the conviction that by such investments, England employs her annua! surplus of capital both safely and binds more closely the ties of mutual interest between the two countries. Hut if the whole scheme of internal improvements in the Union is to be carried into elfect on the vast scale, and with the rapidity lately projected, and by

the means of foreign capital, a more comprehensive guarantee than that of individual States will be required to raise so large an amount in a short time. A national pledge would undoubtedly collect capital together from all parts of Europe ; but the forced sales of loans made separately by all the individual states in reckless competition, through a number of channels, render the terms more onerous for all lower the reputation of American credit, and (as reliance is almost exclusively placed on the London market) produce temporary mischief here, by absorbing the floating capital, diverting money from regular business, deranging banking operations, and producing an unnatural balance of trade against this country. It would seem, therefore, as if most of the States must either pause in the execution of their works of improvement, or some general system of combination must be adopted. All corporation stocks are neglected, nor do we hear of any transactions in Hank shares, except in those of the United States Bank. We have the honor to be vour ob't. servant, EARING, BROTHERS & GO.

The lord mayor and lady mayoress again opened their hospital mansion, on Tuesday evening, for the entertainment of their fellow citizens, and to give to several foreigners of distinction, now in this country some idea of the manner in which the citv of London can support its character and hospitality. The marshal and other of officers appeared in their full state dresses, and proceeded the company to the splendidly fitted lip banqueting room. Rich catidclubius, containing a

The whole of the city plate, as well as the lord mayor's private plate, covered the tables, which were adorned with other decorations, useful as well as ornamenlly, for they groaned under all the delicacies of the season. On the right of the lord mavorsat the Hon. Daniel Webster, a member of the Senate of of the United States on the left of his lordship sat Alexander Stewart, Esq. a member of the house of legislature of Nova Scotia. Amongst the company we observed merchants and bankers, the deputy and common council of the ward of Castlebavnard, and some of the inhabitants of that ward, not of the corporation, several clergymen and other gentlemen. After the usual loyal and patiiotic toasts were drunk, the Lord Mayor rose to propose The health of Mr. Webster," a learn- " ed and distinguished member of the Senate of a country in whose welfare the great city of London, and indeed the whole of the British empire, were at that moment most extensively interested. Allied as the two countries were, in a mercantile point of view, there was no English merchant, banker, or tradesman, who did not look at the daily journals with feeliogs of self-interests with regard to its monetary condition, for that which could shake or destroy the credit of the one country must more or less affect the other þÿ (hear, hear.) When convulsions were allowed to take place in public credit, and confidence was allowed to lie shaken, it was

difficult to say who might not bo involved in the consequences. That America, of all countries in the world, should be laboring under difficulties of a pecuniary nature, certainly surprised him. A country without a national debt, with a surplus income of more than a million of money above its expenditure, should he though be a happy and a nourishing country. The British merchant must have confidence and give to the Americans that consideration which he would wish lo have conceded to himself under similar circumstances, and all would be well þÿ (hear, hear ) Anxious to keep peace with the mother country in improvements, they had borrowed money to such an extent as, for a time, to turn the balance against them ; but he felt assured that confidence was ail that was required, and the result would prove to be in every way satisfactory þÿ (applause.) Mr. Whbster said that he was greatly indebted to the lord inayer, and that he felt highly honored by the invitation which he had received froin his lordship and the ladv mayoress to their hospitable mansion. He was much gratified by the manner in which his health had been proposed in so large and respectable an assembly as he then saw around him þÿ (applause ) He had been some time in England, arid it was one of his wishes, before he returned, to become acquainted with the citizens of London þÿ the first city in the world. The more ho had seen of the institutions of this country, the more delighted that he had an opportunity of witnessing the

magnificence of its capit. 1 city and tfie hospitality of the grand residence of its chief magistrate, (applause.) He begged to he allowed to trespass with a few words upon the patience of the lord mayor and the citizens of London, lie was reminded that the extent and lalue of the commercial intercourse between England and the United States, were twenty-fold greater than with the powerful neighboring kingdom of France; and that although seperalcd by the atlanlic ocean, through the improvements of science applied

to their navigation, they were now no more then 12 days distan re from each oilier. þÿ ll was|the tics of blood and descent, of good feeling liberty, and kindred institutions, which endeared the American of the English people to those who occupied the land of their common forefathers, appluse.) Of the institutions of this country he could not now trust himself to speak; but he must advert to the basis of most of tliem þÿ a basis securing success, founded on pure religion. Long might they exist and prosper, and exist arid prosper they would, (cheers.) He then observed that, had it not been for the lady mayoress's presence he should have begged permission, before he sat down, to have given a sentiment as a toast, and it should have been "Prosperity to the City of London," for he felt that its welfare was dear toeverv American bosom, as it was to fiis own; but at the present moment he would waive it for one which he desired to be the medium of proposing to the company and in which he felt confident of meeting with a responsive feeling þÿ "The Health of the Lady Mayoress." A Russian Wedding. þÿ I had a very natural wish to see a Russian wedding, and it was soon gratified. Count , brother to him whom I had the pleasure to know in Paris, very kindly invited me to accompany him the other evening to the marriage of Col ., with Mademoiselle . The history of the parties was simple enough, and too frequent, perhaps, in all countries ; it was a marraige de covenance. "We found the chapel brilliantly lighted up ; two small altars were raised iu the centre, on which wore placed the cup of wine, two coronets of gold, the holy gospel, and consecrated image, which was afterwards to be removed to the nuptial chamber. The mutual friends were assembled, and formed a circle in their usual dress, the relations only being in full uniform with their cordons and decorations. The bridegroom arrived first, and joined the gioup, who were eager to express their congratulations on the occasion ; in a short time appeared the bride, attended by her family and the usual attendants. It would be rare to see a handsomer person ; she was dressed in white,

They were placed before the altars iu face of the pope ; to each was given a lighted taper, and the service began with a chorus from the chantres de. la our. During this commencement the bride appeared much agitated : but she soon mastered her emotion, though the heaving bosom and trembling taper still gave evidence of the internal struggle The questions and replies together with the interchange of rings, eor- O respond with the rites of other churches; but llieie is one ceremony peculiar to the Greek church, which is at once symbolical and affecting. The pope takes the cup of wine, and invites the betrothed pair to drink of it alternately, a taeit engagement to share in as common the good and evil of their future lives; this idea is also renewed, when they walk three times round the altars, artn-in-arm, while the golden coronets are held over their heads by the assistants. þÿ The benediction is then pronounced, the new married couple are led to the holv place, where they kiss the pictures of the saints, and the ceremonv is finished. In any other country it would be supposed, that when a lovely person, like Mile. w is sacrificed at the altar by her friends, their object must have been to secure a rich and noble husband for a portionless daughter- But tins was not the case ; she had an independent fortune, and her future husband had

neither title, connections, nor a ruble beyond his pay. But here the epaulette is every tiling. He was a colonel in the army, and military rank is the only acknowledged grade in the Slate; she was thrown into the arms of a man. her inferior in every point, with her leeliugs perhaps already devoted to another, solely and simply that she might acquire an ascertained rank in the scale of Russian society þÿ Ha ike's City of the Czar.

Influence of Women. þÿ A writer in the New- York Review, speaking of the Roman women, and their influence during the existence of the kingdom, says: þÿ "From the time of the Subines to Theodora's conquest of J ustinian, women seem to have been at the bottom of almost all the memorable events of Roman story, Lucrctia, Virginia, Veluria. Where Hudson's wave, o'er silvery sands, Winds through the hills afar, Old Cro'nest like a monarch stands, Crowned with a single star: And there, amid the billowy swells Of rock-ribbed, cloud-capt earth, My fair and gentle Ida dwells, A nymph of mountain birth. The snow curl that the cliff receives, The diamonds of the showers, Spring s tender blossoms, buds and leaves, The sisterhood of flowers, Morn s early beam, eve's balmy breeze, Her purity define ; But Ida's dearer far than these To this fond breast of mine. My heart is on the hills. Mr. Fox to Mr. Forsyth. VV vshinuton, January 20. 1810. The undersigned, her Britannic Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, has the honor to acquaint Mr. Forsvth, Secretary of State of the United Slates that since the date of his last official note of the 12th instant, he has been furnished by her Majesty's authorities in North America with more correct information than he then possessed, respecting certain reported movements of British troops within the disputed territory, which formed the subject of a part of that official note, as well as of the two official notes addressed by the Secretary of State to the undersigned on the 21th of December, and on the 16tb of the present month. The same reported movements of troops were referred to in a recent message from the Governor of Maine to the Legislature of the State, and also in a published official letter addressed bv the Governor of Maine to the President of the United States, on the 23d of December. It appears from accurate information now I in the possession of the undersigned, that the Governor of Maine, and through Inm the President and general government of the United States, have been misinformed as to the facts. In the first place no reinforcement has been marched to the British post at the Lake Temiscouata; the only change occurring I there has been the relief of a detachment of her Majesty's 24th regiment by a detachment 1 of equal force of the 1 1th regiment þÿ this force of one company being stationed at the Tc-

3>AIT3JE Ta3T3ST3»a33: ®305»3s3iT©3 AT33. miscouata post, as it always has been, for the necessary purpose of protecting the stores and accommodations provided for the use of her Majesty's troops, who may be required, as heretofore, to march by that route to and from the provinces of Canada and New Brunswick. In the stcond place, it is not true that the British authorities either have built, or are building, barracks on both sides of St. John's river, or at the mouth of the Madawaska river; no new barracks have in fact been built any where. In the third place, her Majesty's authorities are not concentrating a military force at the Grand Falls. The same trilling force of sixteen men is now stationed at the post of the Grand Falls, which has been stationed there for the lust twelvemonth. It was perhaps, however, needless for the undersigned to advert to this last matter at all, as the post of the Grand Falls is beyond the bounds ol the disputed territory, and within the acknowledged limits of New Brunswick. The undersigned, while conveying J c3 the above information, upon a matter of fact, to the Secretary of State of the United Slates, takes occasion to repeat distinctly his former declaration, that there eists no intention on the part of Her Maj sty's authorities to infringe the terms of those provisional agreements which were entered into at the beginning of last year, so long as there is reason to trust that the same will be faithfully adhered to by the opposite party. But it is the duty of the undersigned, at the same time, clearly

to state that her Majesty's authorities in North America, taking into view the attitude assumed by the State of Maine with reference to the boundary question, will, as at present advised, be governed entirely by circumstances in adopting such measures of defence and protection, (whether along the confines of the disputed territory, or within that portion of it where it has been before explained, the authority of Great Britain, according to the existing agreements, was not to be interfered with.) as may seem to them necessary tor guarding against, or for promptly repelling, the farther acts of hostile aggression over the whole of the disputed territory, which it appears to be the avowed design of the Stale of Maine sooner or later to attempt. For the undersigned has to observe, that not only is the extensive system of encroachment, which was denounced and remonstrated against by the undersigned in his official note of the 2d of last November, still carried on and persisted in by armed bands, employed by the authorities of Maine in the districts above the Aroostook and Fish rivers, but that acts, as above stated, of a character yet more violent and obnoxious to the rights of Great Britain, and more dangerous to the preservation of the general peace, are with certainty meditated by the inhabitants of that state. þÿ The existence of such designs has for months past been a matter of notoriety by public report: those designs were plainly indicated in the recent measure of the Governor of Maine

to the Legislature of the state ; and they are avowed in more explicit terms in the letter addressed to the President of the United States by the Governor of Maine, on the 21st of November, which letter has, within the last few days, been communicated to Congress and published. The undersigned, it is true, has been assured by the Secretary of Slate, in his note of the 16th instant, that the general govern-

ment see no reason to doubt the dispositiot of the Governor of Maine to adhere to tl,existing arrangements, and to avoid ail act? tending to render more difficult and distai the final adjustment of the boundary questioi But in face of the above clear indications <> the intentions of Maine, as given out by th. parties themselves, the Secretary of Stab has not given to the undersigned any ad< quate assurance that Maine will be constrain ed to desist from carrying those intentions into effect, if, contrary to the expectation o> j the general government, the Legislature o: the Executive of the state should think lit tc make the attempt. The undersigned not only preserves tin hope, but he entertains the firm belief, that ii the duty of negotiating the boundary questioi be left in the hands of the two national Gov ernments, to whom of right it belongs, the difficulty of conducting the negotiation to ar amicable issue will not be found so great ar has been by many persons apprehended. Bu' the case will become wholly altered, if th' people of the State of Maine, who, though interested in the result, are not charged wit! the negotiation, shall attempt to interrupt i< by violence. Her Majesty's authorities in North Ameri ca have, on their part, no desire or intention to interfere with the course of the pending negotiation, by an exertion of military force; but they will, as at present advised, consult their own discretion in adopting the measures of defence that may be rendered necessary b\

the threats of a violent interruption to the j negotiation which have been used by al parties in Maine, and which the undersigned regrets to find confirmed by the language (as above referred to) employed by the highest official authority in that slate. The undersigned avails himself of this oc. casion to renew to the Secretary of State of I the United States the assuiance of his dis tinguished consideration. (Signed) H. S. FOX. The Hon. John Forsyth, &.c. &c. &c.

Mr. Forsyth, to Mr. Fox. Department of State, Washington, 28th Jan 1840. The undersigned, Secretary of State of the1 United States, has the honor to reply, by direction of the President, to the note addressed to him on the 26th instant, by Mr. Fox, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of Great Britain. The President derives great satisfaction from the information conveyed by Mr Fox's note, that with reference to the reported movements of British troops within the territory in dispute, no actual change has taken place in the attitude of her Majesty's authori- 1 tics in the territory, since the arrangements entered into by the two governments at the commencement of last year, for the preservation of tranquility within its limits; and from his assurances that there exists no intention on the part of her Majesty's authorities to infringe the terms of those arrangements, so j long as they arc faithfully observed on the side of the United States The President, however, cannot repress a 1 feeling of regret that the British colonial au- 1 thorities, without graver motives than the possibility of a departure from the arrangements referred to, bv the stale of Maine should take upon themselves the discretion and, along with it, the tearful responsibility of probable consequences, of being guided by

ci.cuoisiances, liatde as these are t«> be misapprehended and misjudged, in the adoption I? within the disputed territory of measures of defence and precaution, in manifest violation, of the understanding between the two countries, whenever they imagine that acts of 5 hostile a gression over the disputed territory are meditated or threatened on the part of the | stale of Maine. The President cannot but hope that, when her Majesty's Government at home shall be apprised of the position assumed in this regard by its colonial agents, proper steps will be taken to plac e the pet fornianee of express and solemn agreements upon a more secure basis than colonial discretion, to be exercised on apprehended dis.egard o£ i such agreements on the part of the state of Maine. It is gratifying to the President to perceive that Mr Fox entertains the (inn belief that the diifieulty of conducting to an amicable issue the pending negotiation for the adjustment of the question cd boundary is not so great as has, by mariv persons, been apprehended. As. under a corresponding conviction, the United Stales have, with a view to the final settlement of that exciting question, submitted a proposition for the considciation of the Majesty's Government, the President hopes that the sentiments expressed by Mr' Fox have their foundation in an expectation of his having it in his power at an early dav to communicate to this Government a result of the deliberations bad hv that of her Hntannic Majesty upon the proposition alluded to

which will present the piospeci of a prompt and satisfactory settlement, and winch, when known by the State of Maine, will put an end to all grounds of apprehension of intentions or disposition on her part to adopt any measure calculated to embarrass the negotiation) or to involve a departure from the provisional arrangements. In the existence of those arrangements, the United States behold an earnest of the mutual desire of the two governments to divest a question, abounding in causes of deep and growing excitement, of as much as possible of the asperity and hostile feeling it is calculated to engender ; but unless attended with lite most scrupulous observance of the spirit and letter of their provisions, it would prove but one more cause added to the many already prevailing, of enmity and discord. Mr. box lias already been made the channel of conveyance to bis government ol the desire and determination of the President that the obligations of the country shall be faithfully discharged ; that desire is prompted by a sense of expediency as well as of justice, and by an anxious wish to preserve the amicable relations now, so manifestly lor the advantage of both, subsisting between the United .States and Great Britain. The undersigned avails himself of the occasion to renew to Mr. Fox assurances of his distinguished consideration. (Signed) JOHN FOltSYTH.

On Saturday Governor Porter sent a special message to the Legislature of Pennsylvania, on the subject of the State Loan, the finances, &c He announces that the State loan authorised by a recent act, for the purpose of meeting the payment of «s6t,'0,000 due as interest on the State debt, cannot be negotiated at present. Various Banks ot Philadelphia offered to loan portions according to their means, and others declined on account of inability. After announcing these facts, the Governor adds þÿ | " It will be perceived that, not having the means so to do, the interest this day due by the Commonwealth to her creditors is unpaid, a circumstance winch the Executive, anxious as he has been for maintaining unsullied the credit of the Commonwealth, has been unable J to avert." To preserve the credit of the Slate Gov. Porter recommends, as " the best alternative which can present itself, the passage forthwith of a joint resolution authorising the issuing of State stock for the interest now due' to be delivered to the holders of the stock for the amount due them respectively." This is intended as an earnest of the determination of ? the State oovernment to make provision, as soon as the necessary legislation can be had i| to meet the exigency and redeem the credit of the commonwealth. ! The message contains a declaration, interesting and important in the present stale o' things at Harrisburg, relative to the resumption of specie payments. Governor Porter says ; þÿ " No man, where he concerned alone as

an individual, would go further to fix an early day for the resumption of specie payments by the Banks than 1 would, if by so doing the if desirable results would be produced. But. placed as I am, as the Fsecutioc of the Commonwealth, to preside over her interests. I feel bound to say, regardless of any denunciation which may be poured forth from any quarter, that I believe if too rigorous a system of measures be adopted to coerce the payment of the liabilities of the ban'. s, immediately, the credit of the State must and will be seriously and disastrously affected

The Lexington þÿ Inquest. ninth and last day After nine days of laborious investigation, this melancholy case was brought to a close last evening. þÿ The coroner charged the jury, leaving with them all the documents which had been in evidence before them. At 6 o'clock in the evening it was annouu. ced that they had agreed, and they then caine in with the following VERDICT. " That the deceased, Stephen Waterbury, Philo Upson, Silas Thorburn, Benjamin Lader and Jacob C. Bates, came to their death in
IF.
consequence of the burning of the steamboat Lexington, in Longs Island Sound on the 13th instant." The jury also appended to their verdict the following PRESENTMENT.

From the testimony adduced before the court of inquiry by the coroner's inquest, to investigate the causes which led to the destruction by tire of the steamboat Lexington, the inquest are of opinion that the fire was communicated to the promenade deck by the intense heat of the smoke pipe, or from sparks from the space between the smoke pipe and steam chamber, as the fire was first seen near the casing of the steam chimney above the promenade deck. They are farther of opinion that the Lexington was a first rate boat, with an excellent steam engine, and a boiler suitable for burning wood, but not coal, with the blowers attached. Furthermore it is our opinion, that had the buckets been maimed at the commencement of the fire, it could have been immediately extinguished. Also, inasmuch as the engiue could not be stopped, from the rapid progress of the lire, with presence of mind of the officers, and a strict discipline of the crew, the boats could have been launched, and a large portion of the psasengers and crew, if not the whole, might have been saved. It is the opinion of this jury, that the present inspectors of steamboats, either from ignorance or neglect, have sulleied the steamboat Lexington to navigate the Sound at the imminent risk of liie lives and property ot the passengers, giving a certificate stating a full compliance with the laws of the United States, while in our opinion such was not the case. That the system as adopted on board the Lexington, ' of using blowers on board of boats, O O

is dangerous, as has been proved to the jury by competent witnesses And that the eonduct of the officers of the steamboat Lexington, on the night of the 13th of January, wtien said steamboat was on tire, deserves the severest censure of this community ; li om tbe facts proved before this jury, ifial the captain and pilot, in the greatest hour of danger, loft the steamboat to her own guidance, and sought their own safety, rcgaidless of the fate of the passengers; instead of the captain or pilot retreating to the tiller, all, when driven front the wheel house, forward, and the ropes iheie being burned off, their being at that time a communication to lite said uilei, there appeared tube no olbei thought but sell pieservation. And it farther appears to this jury, that the odious practice ot carrying cotton in any quantities on boaru of passenger boats, in a manner in which it shad be liable to take tire, from spaiks or beat, from any smoke pipe, or olfier means, deserves the public censure. Signed by James Goadby, Thomas E. Burlew, S. 11 Harriott, Touuis Foskcs, Janus Green, I'. M 1. Durando, Jr., Edmund B. Mc'Veagh, A. S. Chace, Abraham Creveling, Robert Buttler, Richard M, Hoc, Henry V. Davids þÿ 12. FRINGE ALBERT. (Correspondent of a Ministerial paper.) Sir, þÿ As any authentic information at the presentjuncture relative to his serene Highness Prince Albert of Saxe Coburg may be acceptable to you, and interesting to youi readers, 1 forward you some account of an interview 1 was fortunate enough to have with him a short time since. I was on my way home from a Continental tour just at the period his Highness was about to sail from Antwerp to London, to pay a visit to our most gracious Soverign, and came in the same boat, the Antwerpen. Our pas sage was considerable lengthened by a seri ous accident which happened to one of the engines of the vessel, and we were actually stationary on the Scheldt for nearly five hours, &. should not then have been able pru- ' dently to proceed to London had not the fine sieaiiier Princess Victoria (apropos enough) been put in requisition to tow us across the channel. This circumstance gave me the more time and opportunity to observe and converse with the Prince. He manifested great presence of mind when the accident happened, which was really, for some minutes, very alarming. He entered into conversaiion on a variety of subjectsjn the most affable and intelligent manner, and convinced me that he possessed a well-regulated and refined mind, rather calculated for, and dispo sed to philosophical subjects He appeared kind hearted and humane; this 1 collected from his conduct to one of the servants of the I suiie, who unfortunately fell down the hold of

the vessel, and was considerably hurt ; and f also from other circumstances of too miunte a nature for detail. His Highness is in stature rather above the middle-height, exceedingly well proportioned, and of very manlv appearance for his years þÿ 1 should have taken him for f twenty four or twenty-five ; his general manner is easy, unaffected, and graceful ; his features are regular, well defined, and exceeding- , Iv English ; his countenance is open, its ex press, on mild, and there is a certain inexpres sib! something above his light smiling evesj which s: ,os at once to inspire esteem and con- j fi leitce It was this which encouraged me' to address him more frequently than 1 otherwise would have done. If you think the above likely to be acceptable to the public, or any part of it, it is at your service. > -- « fv » w- From the Guiana Chronicle. January 20.

Joint sloe'. Banks in Ln gland. þÿ A return has been published on the subject of jointstock banks, for the three years ending 1838. It appe rs tint the increase in the number of these ctanbsoineiits in England was extremely rapid m 1336. In that year it received a chc k. and on the 1st of January. 1839, the iitimher was less by three than in January, 1«38 þÿ The whole number of joint-stock banks in England at 1st January last was 1(»3, Of these 1 1 were established between 1826 and 18215, both inclusive. They were 22 established in the five years from 1830 to 1-331. No less than 67 were established in 1 835 and 1836. They were 7 established in 1837, and 1 in 1838. The number of part, nets varies front 50 to 1.200. and may average about 300- There are half a dozen with less than filtv partners, the smallest number being seven. Fifty eight of the banks have branches, and 50 have none, þÿ The branches, including the parent bank, are from 2 to 67 in number. There are 8 banks which have

>ort than 20 brarttihes. The whole number >f parent banks and branches is 608. There ,ie besides about 550 private banks in Engm,l, that is, banks having no more than G tanners. Adding these to the joint stock lanks and their branches, the whole number t banking establishments will be about 1,200. \ccording to the last return, dated 2d August, the notes in circulation of all the jointstork banks were in value £4,005,1 10. This, li vided-by the number of banks (108), gives in average circulation of only £43,200 lor ach ; or, if we include the branches, theaverige for each office or establishment is only £8,000. Supposing the money to be employed in discounting at five per cent, the nnual profit on £4,605,000 would be only £230,000, or no more than £350 to each establishment It is evident that their profits must be chiefly derived from deposits, which thev can employ at five per cent, while, we believe, they give only two. The issues of the private banks, by the same return, were £7,610,700, which gives an average of about £14,000 for each establishment. It appears that the joint-stock banks, so far from superseding the private banks, have but a very slight effect in narrowing their issues.

Account nf the North Cape, the moat Northern land in Europe, where the Sun never sets. The North Cape is an enormous rock, which projecting far into the ocean, and, being exposed to all the fury of the waves, and the outrage of tempests, crumbles every year more and more into ruins þÿ Here every thing is solitary, every thing is sterile, very sad and despondent. The shadow forest no longer adorns the brow of the mountain; the singing of the birds, which enliven even the woods of Lapland, is no longer heard in this 1 scene of desolation; the ruggedness of the Idark gray rock is not covered by a single I shrub ; the only music is the hoarse murmur- ing of the waves, ever and anon renewing their assaults on the huge masses that oppose them. The northern sun, creeping at midnight at the distance of five diameters along the horizon, and the immeasurable ocean in |i apparent contact with the skies, form the grand outlines in the sublime picture presented e> the astonished spectator. '1 lie incesj sant cares and pursuits of anxious mortals ; are recollected as a dream ; the various forms j and energies of animated nature are forgoti ten; the earth is contemplated only in its ele- I inents. and as constituting a part of the solar 'system, Having mad: drawings of those I rocks under various aspects, we landed from our boat, and scrambled upon the top of tin m. We there found some pieces of wood thrown up by the sea, with which we kindled a fire , in the face of the frozen Ocean, and began to

| prepare a repast In looking about for a . i place to which we might retire vviili some comfort, wc discovered a grotto, formed by 1 three rocks, whose smooth and polished sides indicated that they had heretofore been washed for many ages by the waves of the sea. I In the midst of these rocks was a large roundish stone, under which there ran a small stream of water. As we were tracing the I course of this stream, which had us source in I a neighbouring mountain, we found on its margin some plants ol Angela a. I his wc regarded as a great acquisition to our refresh- because wc had found it to bo a very table, ing and salubrious vegetable. The grotto was so convenient, that it had the appeal. tni.e

of being the work of art. The stone in the centre served for a table, around which we could place ourselves ; and we had only to stoop down to replenish our bowl with water perfectly Iresh and sweet, though we were within a few paces of the salt sea. We regretted much that we had no iron implement wherewith to engrave some motto, oral least our names, on those rocks.

MEANS FOR THE PRESERVATION OF THE KING OF FRANCE. The following description of the means taken to preserve the King of France from personal outrage and h.s palace from attack, is from the Paris Commerce. It possesses an interest superior to that of common Parisian gossip. Louis Philippe is in more senses than one a King of the Barricades. " The service of the Palace was never more rigorous than at present at any former period, or in any other reign. The soldiers themselves are terrified by it. Our readers remember the fate of the poor man who was killed for having too closely approached the gate of the Rue de Rivoli. Ever since, additional precautions have been taken, the military garrison of the l'uileries is obliged to take the same measures, and is as touch on the qui vice as if it were in presence of the enemy. " There are round the Palace thiee principal lines of defence, included between the Seme, the Square of Louis X t ., the Rue de Rivoli, and the Place de Carrousel. The river closes on one side that extensive polygon ; too deep to be found ; its bridges, adjoining the L'uileries, form defiles Uilfieult of access. " The paralled line comprises the different debouches of the streets of L'Eehelle, St. Roch, and Rivoli, and is much better supported than that of the Carrousel. " Two military governors are installed at the Louvre and in the Tuilerics respectively. They combine their operations, create, modify, and interpret their consigns, and are able, by their military knowledge, to organize at a

moment a system of defence. ' The arms of the soldiers on duty are every where loaded. " The guard formed of companies of picked men, who are reviewed daily, of National Guards and of Cavalry. " During the day several distiuct secret sets of police keep watch on each other, and are in continual movement along the lines þÿ This service is even organized amidst the crowd of the public, follows its undulations, and marches and stops with it. Each mouchard, spy or carries under his coat a belt, in which are slung a brace ol pistols and a dagger. The 'comrade who relieves him merely makes a sign to him. Agents seated in hackney-coaches are continually reconnoitering the approaches ol the chateau, and a watch, or living telegraph, posted on the top of the j noiso of carriages and oi the galloping root, roof, gives notice notice of ol the approacn approach of oi any ihinu calculated to disturb the dynastic order. " These precautions are redoubled toward nightfall. Three hundred and fitly picked men, supplied by all tbe regiments ot tne garrison, arrive at that hour, and take their station under the I'aviiion ol the Clock.
y rapid succession, ar.d during the night they E cence to within issue from the Palace, and are constantly I pally

met moving round it, along the quays, the Square of Louis XV., the Carrousel, the Ruej de Revoli, and the Rue St. Honore. tions, which are supported by posts, are other reserves stationed "Independently of these military numerous disposi- at th< . j Place des Pyramids and at the Ministry oi j Finanees ; the battalion of infantry quarterei in one of the wings of tbe Palace, and the cavalry barrack on the Q,uai d Orsav ; thos' reserves, placed within short distance of each other, constitute an effective force of betweei 3,000 or 4,000 men, which may he turner I out and concentrated at the Palace in the course of five minutes. The parapets, bridges, railings, the gati are well guarded. The internal defensive measures are still more formidable. A ditel limits the garden ; the area of the gate ol the J'avilion de I' Horloge has been raised iuordt i to render its approach the more difficult ; thchimnies have been secured by iron bar across them ; double doors of solid oak, and turning easily on enormous hinges are pet art! \ (or bomb) proof; the cellars and subienune ous passages are guarded in such a maunet I that any attempt to undermine trie paiace | would prove abortive ; and certain cabinetwhich are as strong as casements, are tra- , versed bv a small winding staircase, extend- , irig from the cellar to the roof ; 150 servants, j officers, and sergeants of experienced courage, dressed during the day-time in a handsome uniform, throw it off at nignt. About half a dozen years ago, a very worthy farmer in a neighbouring State used to come to this village weekly to sell his " produce " He soon found that it was much easier to sell than to get payment. Among others he trusted a widow 2 or 3 dollars. þÿ He dunned and dunned her until he began to feel somewhat vexed þÿ not angry, for the lady was very lavish of her smiles, and managed the affair so adroitly, that the creditor almost resolved to 'grin and bear it' After no little reflection he determined to make one more effort ; knowing that every person has a weak spot, he thought that if he could discover Iter's and attack it with all his force, she would surrender, and he get his debt. He called on Saturday, ran into the

kitchen where she was at work ; her looks bespoke confusion, hut recovering presence of mind, she with all the ease of a school hoy who has repeated his lesson for the filtielh time, said, " Why Mr. 1 am very glad to see you but I can't pay you to day ; you must call next week." "Oh my clear madam,'! replied he, 1 did " not come to talk about that ; 1 did not even think of that sum I'm come on what is more important to my happiness, and 1 trust to vour's þÿ Madam (here he directed a most killing look at her) madam 1 am a widower." þÿ Here he paused, as if his rising feelings choked his struggling voice. The widow instinctively felt what the widower was aiming at> and ought not to be censured il she attempted to meet him half way. She ordered her youngest daughter to go to the factory and ask the agent for the money he promised her. Then the good woman retired to the adjoining room, where she placed on her head a fashionable cap, and arrayed herself in a new silk gown. Having given the last glance in a looking glass, she was satisfied that no man, or rather no widower could withstand the combined influences of her ' form divine" and beautiful dress. She entered the room and seated herself in the chair next to her loving creditor, prepared to receive his proposals. At this important juncture, between hope and doubt, the little girl returned with the money. Tha lady now paid the debt ; the gentleman pocketed the money took his hat and walked out of the house, murmuiing to himself, that there was more

than one way to collect a debt. Every one can imagine how the widow bit her lips with shame and anger, when she learnt that the pietended widower had at that lime a very fine wilt and a number of promising children ! She was mad, indeed ! and to spite him. she declared in her wisdom that she would never ask him to trust her again for his good foruothing trash. þÿ Pawtucket Chronicle.

We publish to-day from the Globe of Wednesday evening, the recent correspondence between Governor Fairfield, Mr Forsyth and Mr Fox, on the subject of the "military possession" alleged to have been recently taken of the disputed territory, or of that portion lying adjacent to the Temiscouata l.uke. The facts, as discloseu by this correspondence, do certainly very most essentially from the representation made by Mr. Fox in the correspondence ol January ; it is undeniable t hat a military possession has been taken þÿ on a small scale, to be sute, but still a military possession þÿ that is, the permanent posting of troops, the erection or other preparation of barracks. &c., and the construction of military roads. The force now admitted by Mr. Fox to be stationed at Temiscouata Lake, is about 175 men, exclusive of officers ; and a late number of the St. John Courier states that a reinforcement of '250 men has been ordered thither, and that Col. Goldie has been ordered to the command of the station. But we do not charge Sir John Harvey with a violation of his agreement ; and under the circumstances of the case, it seems to us that a more judicious as well as more candid and honorable course for Mr. Fox to pursue, would be to admit at once the military possession, and justify it by the terms of Sir John Harvey's agreement. W« have been looking at that document and have discovetod a clause in it which completely exonerates the Lieut Governor of New Brunswick, and to our mind furnishes

a key to the whole mystery of the recent proceedings on his part. The stipulation entered into by him was in these words: þÿ " That it is not the intention of the Lieut Governor of New Brunswick, under the expected renewal of negotiations between the cabinets of London and Washington on the subject of the disputed territory, without renewed i ash actions to that effect from Ins govermnenl , to seek to take military possession," Ate. By the force of the words in italics, it will be seen, die operation of the agreement was expressly limited to Sir John Harvey ; it was not binding either on the British Government or on Sir John Harvey's immediate superior, ces. If renewed instructions to take mili- the Governor General of the British provin- " tary possession" were given him, he was at liberty to obey them ; and our opinion is that they have been given.
