By the direction of the President, the undersigned Secretary of State of the United Slates, communicates to Mr. Pox, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of Groat Britain, the enclosed copy ol a report made to the Governor of the State of Maine, by the agent, commissioned on the part of the authorities of that State, to ascertain the precise character and extent of the occupation of parts of the disputed territory by troops of her Britannic Majesty, and of the buildings and other public works constructed tor their use and accommodation By that report, and the three depositions which the undersigned informally communicated to Mr. Fox, a few days since, he will perceive that there must be some extraordinary misapprehension on his part of the facts in relation to the occupation by British troops of portions of the disputed territory þÿ I he statements contained in these documents, and that given by Mr. Fox, in his note ol the 26th of January last, exhibit a striking discrepancy as to the number of troops now in the territory, as compared with those who were in u when the arrangement between Governor Fairfield and Lieutenant Governor Harvev was agreed upon ; and also as to the present and former state of the buildings there.--The extensive accommodations prepared and preparing, at old and at new stations, the works finished, and in the course of construction, on the land and on the water,

are not in harmony with the assurance that the onlv object is the preservation of a few unimportant buildings and storehouses, for tho temporary protection of the number of troops her Majesty's ordinary service can require to pass on the road front New Brunswick hack to Canada. The undersigned will abstain from any remarks upon these contradictory statements, until Mr. Fox shall have had an opportunity to obtain the means ol fully explaining them. How essential it is that this should be promptly done, and that the steps necessary to a faithful observance on the part of liar Majesty's colonial authorities of the existing agreements between the two governments, should be immediately taken, Mr. Fox cannot fail fully to understand. The undersigned avails himself of the occasion to renew to Mr. Fox assurances of his high consideration. JOHN FORSYTH.

Mr. Fox to Hr. Forsyth Washington. March 7, 1840. The undersigned, her Britannic Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, has the honor to acknowledge the receipt of the official note of yesterday's date, addressed to him by Mr. Forsyth, Secretary of Slate of the United States, to which is annexed tho copy of a report from Mr. Benj. Wiggin. an agent employed bv the Slate of Maine to visit the British military post at Lake Temiscouata ; and in which reference is made to other papeis upon the same subject, which were informally communicated to the undersigned by Mr. Forsyth, a few days before ; and the attention of the undersigned is called by Mr. Forsyth to different points upon which the information contained in the said papers is considered to he materially at variance with that which was conveyed to the United States Government by the undersigned, in his official note of the 2(5th of last January. The undersigned had already been made acquainted, by the Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick, with the circumstance of Mr. þÿWiggin s visit to the military post at Lake Temiscouata, where the officer in command very properly furnished to Mr. W iggin the requisite information upon all matters connected with the British station, which he appeared desirous to inquire about. The alleged points of variance, after deducting what is fanciful and conjectural in the reports now produced, anti after comparing what is there staled in contradiction to

other reports before produced from the same quarters, do not appear to the undersigned to be bv any means so material as they seem to have been considered by the Government of the United States. The British military detachment stationed at Lake Temiscouta, which the agents employed by the state ol Maine had, in the first instance, with singular exaggeration, represented as amounting to two regiments, is now discovered by the same parties to amount to one hundred and seventv five men, which iustead ol two regiments, is something less than two companies. It is indeed true, should such a point be considered worth discussing, that the undersigned might have used a more technically correct expression in his note of the 26th of January, if he has stated the detachment in question to consist of from one to two companies, instead of staling it to consist ol one company. But a detachment of her þÿMajesty troops s has been stationed at the lake Temiscouata, from time to lime, ever since the winter of 183 and '38, when the necessity arose front marching reinforcements bv that route from New Brunswick to Canada ; and it will be remembered that a temporary right of using that route tor the same purpose, was expressly reserved to Great Britain in the provisional agreement entered into at the beginning of last year. It is not, therefore, true, that the stationing a military force at the lake Temiscouata is a new measure on the part of her þÿMajesty s authorities Neither is it true that that mea-

sure has been adopted for other purposes titan to maintain the security of the customary line of communication, and to protect the buildings, stores, and accommodations provided for the use of Her þÿMajesty troops s when on a march by that route ; and it was with a view to correct misapprehensions which appeared to exist upon these points, and thus to do away with one needless occasion of dispute, that the undersigned conveyed to the United States Government the information contained in his note of the 26th January. With regard to the construction of barracks and other buildings, and the preset ving them in an efficient state of repair and defence, a similar degree of error and misapprehension appears still to prevail in the minds of the American authorities The erection of those buildings within the poition of the disputed territory now referred to, for the shelter ot her Majesty 's troops while on their march, and tor the safe lodgment of tho stores, is no new act on the part of her Majesty's authorities. The buildings in question have been in the course of construction from a period antecedent to the provisional agreements of last year, and they are now maintained and occupied along the line of march, with a view to the same objects above specified, for which the small detachments of troops also referred to, are in like manner there stationed. The undersigned will not refrain from here remarking upon one point ot comparison exhibited in the present controversy It is ad-

mitted by the United States authorities that the armed bands stationed by the Government of Maine in the neighborhood of the Aroostook river, have fortified those stations with artillery ; and it is now objected as matter of complaint against the British authorities, with reference to the buildings at Luke Tern iscouata, not that these buildings are furnished with artillery, but only that they are defended bv palisades capable of resisting artillery It would be difficult t<> adduce stronger evidence of the acts on the one side being those ot aggression, and on the other of defence. The fact, shoitly, is, and this is the essential point of the argument, that her þÿMajesty s authorities have not as vet altered their state of preparation, or strengthened their military means within the disputed territories, with a view to setting the question of the boundary, although the attitude assumed by the state of Maine with rcfeience to the question, would he a clear justification of such measures; and it is much to he apprehended that the adoption of such measures will sooner or later become indispensable, it the people of Maine he not compelled to desist from the extensive system of armed aggression which they are contin-

AVm uing to carry on in other parts of the satne disputed territory. The undersigned avails himseif of this occasion to renew to the Secretary of Stale of the United States the assurance of his distinguished consideration. H. S. FOX Mr. Williams, of Maine, after a brief analysis of the evidence now produced, which he contrasted seriatim with the allegations of Mr. Fox m the former coi respondence, proceeded as follows : þÿ Having said what 1 considered to he my duty to Governor Fairfield, the state of Maine, and myself, in reference to litis extraordinary letter of the British minister. 1 would now ask the attention of the Senate to a more important view of the subject By the arrangement entered into in March last between the Governor of Maine and the Lieutenant Governor of New Btunswick. it was agieed that the Lieut. Gov. of New Brunswick, without renewed instructions to that t iled, would not seek to take military possession ot the disputed territory Arc In answer to Gov l airfield's inquiry in Dec. last, as to British troops being stationed within the disputed territory, Sir John Harvey says, that whatever movement of troops may have taken plaec on the side of Lower Canada, have been made by authority superior to þÿmine, &. c. Is it possible that, alter making an arrangement with the Lieut Governor of New Brunswick tor the preservation of peace upon the borders, pending the negotiation on the subject of the boundary, we are now to be told tiiat, while the Lieutenant Governor respects and con-

forms to his own arrangement, his superior may and will do as he pleases ; and is to be permitted to construct strong posts and keep what military force lie thinks proper upon the territory in dispute? Are we quietly to re main in a condition so humiliating ? 1 trust not. And vet this is the position in which we are placed, if we accede to the views taken bv Air. Fox iri his letter of 24th of January last, wliete, speaking of her þÿMajesty s authorities in North America, fie says þÿ þÿ They will, as at present advised, consult, their own discretion in adopting the measures of defence that may he rendered necessary by the threats of a violent interruption to the negoeiation, which have been used by all parties in þÿMaine, Ate. Here we have the avowal of the accredit, ed Minister of her Britannic Majesty to this Government, that her Majesty's authorities in North America, (not the Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick, tor he has made an agreement which forbids his doing unassuming, without the least foundation for such assumption, that Maine threatens, or desires a violent interruption to the negoeiation, will, as at present advived, catsuit their own discretion m adopting measures of defence : and we fiave the prool that, in the exercise of that discretion, those authorities have constructed strong iVlilitarv posts, stationed regular troops and made roads for the transportation of men and military stores within the disputed territory. contrary to agreement, and in violation

of the just rights of the State of Maine. Shall we, can we, submit to such usurpation? to such wrong? If there is a patriotic feeling in the bosom of any American, it will emphatically respond no! Mr VV then alluded to the late message of Sir John Harvey to the Assembly of New Brunswick, in which he expresses great confidence that, upon the arrival in Englaud of the commissioners who recently came out to examine the disputed territory, and upon their report being made to the Ministry at home, such a proposition would be made for the adjustment of the question of boundary as would he satisfactory to this Government þÿ He does not intimate what that proposition will be, or how it will he made satisfactory, hut the Assembly thereupon passed a bill to authorize Governor Harvey to raise a corps of twelve hundred men whenever it might become necessary. Uttr whole borders are being surrounded with military posts and fortifieatinns ; additional troops are being sent into the provinces ; and soldiers and military works are placed within and upon a portion of the territory in d spute.

W/7?/ stick means upon our borders to render proposition satisfactory, who can wonder that Sir John Harvey should feel great confidence that it wmdd prove satisfactory ? þÿ No. 9 Litr C. i Would it not, under such circumstances, be wise to place our frontier in a condition which would enable us to consider and act upon any proposition w hich may be made us with calmness and freedom from coercion ? It is not apparent, while this government is resting in security, relying upon the strong and reiterated declarations of Great Britain of its anxious desire to bring the lending controversy a trout our North eastern boundary to an amicable and just, termination, and conforming to the arrangements for preserving peace on the borders, tiiat the British authorities are steadily and constantly preparing for a different result ? þÿ Shall we be blind to the recent augmentation of troops in the provinces þÿ to the construction of military posts upon our whole Eastern and Northern frontiers þÿ to the making of roads lor the speedy movement of troops, and the erection of buildings for their accommodation ? While Maine, deeply interested in the question of boundary, is looking with intense anxiety upon these extensive preparations for conflict, and is calling upon the General Government to fulfil the constitutional duty of protecting and defending her against foreign encroachment and dismemberment, what has the Government done ? Has it come to her in that wav which would have been most like-

ly to preserve her rights and biing the question to a prompt termination? Is it not the duty of tins Government forthwith to meet the recent movements of Great Britain by corresponding movements on our part ? þÿ Would not surh a course promote the arnicacle and early settlement of the pending dispute And bv so doing, would not the hazard of border conflicts he greatly diminished ? These questions demand the serious and solemn consideration of Congress and the country. Maine does not desire, bv anv act of hers, to bring on a war, but she ought not, and cannot, sorter a portion of her territory long to remain in the military occupation of foreign troops. Once a year regularly, just as the sap begins to run in the big maples, and the snows among the highlands are sending off their annual tribute to the ocean þÿ when there is such a breaking up of ice and frost, and such floods in the streams, that no mortal enemy could get from the St. John's up the Aroostook. or from Mars Hill over towards the eastern Penobscot þÿ we have a flare up in the Maine legislature about the everlasting Eastern Boundary. The legislature of that patriotic state have for three or four annual sesþÿsions commenced in a verv quiet and reflecting mood, but before the þÿ ides of March are past, they get up to a fever heat in this vexed and vexing question. Tim resolutions recently passed by the Senate of Maine look to an immediate settlement, or an appeal to arms. The federal government, hitherto anxious to avoid eollition, is now said to be anxious for a conflict ; and the papers are filled with rumors of sharp and angry diplomatic notes exchanged between the British Minister and the Secretary of State. We know not what credit, if any, should be attached to these rumors of war. But we have no belief that, war will ensue, because neither nation wants a war, and neither is in a condition to prosecute a war. We are aware that there is a party in this country, and a party in England, .who would be glad of war. The one in this country

might be able to sustain itself in power under the outward pressure of such an evil, and that in England would obtain power, under a new ministry which would immediately follow such an event. But neither of these parties have the true interests of their respective lountries at heart, and therefore will not, if
lermitted to plunge the two nations into war.

From Canton. þÿ By the arrival of the Navigator, from Canton, we have received the fol lowing intelligence : From the Canton (Macao) Press, Nov 16 183!) On the night from Tuesday and Wednesday he people understand their true interests, be | tfie Chinese opened their batteries on the shipping at Hongkong. The firing began at about

a MMMMnn half an hour after midnight arid w,as kept up without intermission until aboti' 3 o'clock in the morning, when it ceased, but recommenced at about 3, and was kept lip till day-light, without however doing the slightest damage, not a single ball having hit any of the ships, though some of the shots were heard to pass over the vessels nearest the land. Had their fire been well directed, they might have done much mischief, it being perfectly calm at the time, and the ships consequently unahl® to move out of the range of the guns. At daylight soldiers were seen on the shore removing in great haste and tlie guns seemed also to have been removed, nothing but the hastily thrown up breastworks remaining No attempt was made from the shipping though the Hyacinth was at Hongkong, to land and destroy the forts and batteries, and the fleet remained at anchor all that day and the next night, the weather continuing calm, but on Thursday the greatest part set sail for Toui'.gkoo bay, and were on the next day followed by the remainder, where they are all now anchored. This removal from Hongkong, though it will no doubt be represented by the Chinese as flight from their cannon, had been pre- a viously determined on, in consequence of letters sent by Captain Smith of H M. S. Volage, that only at Tungkoo would the merchant ships henceforward enjoy the protection of the ships of war. Hongkong is described by the captains of the merchant fleet as a much better anchorage, and a representation to allow

the (Let to remain there signed by 35 masters of ships was addressed to capt. Smith, snd also, we believe, to capt. Elliot, but without success; several merchant did the same with a like result. The objection to the anchorsge at Tungkoo bay arises, we hear, from the strong tide which prevail there, which render all communication between the shipping extremely difficult. and from its open situation, which may render an attempt on the part of the Chinese, of firing ilia fleet more unsuccessful than at Hongkong, where is but a slight current. þÿ We know not for what reason Capt. Smith would not listen to the representations made to him, except it he that fie has, as we are told orders from Admiral Maitland, to protect the fleet at Tunghoo.

From Canton. þÿ By the ship Albion, Captain Lovett, arrived yesterday frem Calcutta, we have received files of papers to the 3d of December. We find nothing in them of particular importance The following extracts are all that we can find room for: The Chinese still preserve silence on the affair at Chuenpce, and it is said that the Commissioner, in his repoit to Peking, represented it as having cost the Chinese only 13 lives( and only one vessel destroyed, whilst the English ships suffered severely, one of them having hud two masts shot away, and great number of their men having been killed. Such accounts are very similar to European bulle tins published on like occasions. The truth however is that after the affair of Chuenpee no less then 52 bodies were taken to the town of Hengshan alone, there buried. From ibis some guess may be ventured of the loss suffered by the Chinese Humors of preparations for destroying the fleet at Tungkoo are still aflat, but we cannot learn any thing to rely on with certainly. The Commissioner by some is represented as very ill, hut il is moie likely that before proceeding further, he has written for instructions from Peking.

From the St. James's Chronicle, March 14. A naval correspondent has drawn our attention to a typographical error in our statement of the naval force of which the China expedition is to be composed, which we hasten to correct, bv which we were made to understate considerably our case. The crews of the Blenheim, Melville, and Wellesley alone amounted to 1030 men, and those of the remaining eight ships to almost as many more. The crows of the entire squadron, including those ol the small ships from other stations, will probably amount to about 4000 seamen and marines. It has been inquired why so large a force should be employed against a lew miserable junks, an entire fleet ol which a 28 gun ship and a sloop of war were sufficient to disperse ? To which we reply, that the Americans may not choose to go without tea. because we demand that the Chinese shall not do without opium.

We hare elsewhere given a letter from our private correspondent at Alexandria, dated feh 22. It reports the continued and vigorous preparations of the Pacha for his defence. Me has ordered all the troops at Cairo and CSonrah to march to Alexandria, and has seized on all the boats within bis reach lor the transport of troops. These measures, and a rumour that Ibrahim Pacha was about to march on Constantinople, have created great alarm in Alexandria.

Case of Frost and Others. REMOVAL OF THE CONVICTS. Newport, Feb. 3. þÿ The under sheriffs received a respite during pleasure on Saturday last, which was immediately communicated to the prisoners, who had been very much depressed upon hearing that Thursday next was fixed for their execution. Upon the second respite, however, being given them, they were much elated, and felt confident that a free pardon would follow. In this, however, for the present at least, they are disappointed, as an order was received yesterday for their removal, and in the course of the night they were taken from the gaol to Chepstow, under an escort of Lancers. At Chepstow a steam- vessel was in readiness to convey them to Portsmouth, when they will he pot on board a snip lying there, which will take them to their uliiinate destination, where it is said they are to pass the remain der ol their days, it being understood t hat their punishment is commuted to transportation for life So secret was the removal of the prisoner kept, that it was not known at the gaol at 5 o'clock yesterday afternoon. The Newport and hill people are far from satisfied with the result, as they say, that although transportation is a severe punishment, ye' it is not an example, and they think their sufferings have been iost sight of.

From the London Oh server, February 9, 1840. PROGRESS OF PRINCE ALBER T.

Arrival at Brush lls. þÿ Prince Albert was dressed in plain cloihes. and wore no decorations. His Highness appeared in high health and spirits. Since his last visit to I lie place he seems to have improved, if possible, in that dignified and manly comeliness for which he is certainly more conspicuous ihan any other contemporary prince. These natural advantages would, however, Ire of little comparative estimation in the eyes of the British nation if it were not an undoubted fact that tuere is no young man, let hiin he a prince, a peer, or a private person, whose qualities of heart and mind are more worthy of panegyric All those wor have had the honour of knowing inn speak in the highest terms oi his good sense, firm.i tss, prudence, and nnldaess, and are equally ready to applaud ids acc > u rltahmcnU and una dec ted grace, as iney are ready to hear testimony to the in ire sterling excellencies of his gifted and higiiiv cultivated intellect. Nature has been iavisn to Prince Albert, but, witn a degree of good sense most honouraole to himself and his excellent fattier, they have not alone trusted to ephemeral gifts, for his iiignness's time, from hot hood, has been sedulously occupied in seeking to improve his mind, by combining the study of history, legislation, and political economy, with that of tiie more abstruce sciences, and in cultivating those arts and accomplishments which will, in due time, render turn as fit to hold a conspicuous place in the councils, as he is at present

qualified to some in the court circles of his adopted country. Prince Albert is distinguished for being a devoted son, an affectionate brother, and a faithful friend, and there is no Protestant Prince in Germany who has shown himself more warmly attached to those principles winch his ancestors have invariably supported and fought for from the earliest days of the Reformation. Wise without pedantry, generous without extravagance, prudent without narrowness of mind, and religious without superstition or intolerance, Prince Albert promises to be all that the British nation can desire in the husband of

her Queen, and, please God. in the father of her future Monarch. It therefore may be safely affirmed that it will not be Prince Albert's fault if the domestic happiness of his august consort and the honour and glory ot the British nations are not insured and advanced by his elevation to that exalted position for which no prince in Europe is so admirably qualified. þÿ Gorrespondeut of the Morning Post.

PARIS Thursday, Feb. 13. The new Sugar Bill, which places an equa' duty on colonial and native, is extremely favourable to the colonies, and ruinous for the native growers. The committee appointed by the Chamber of Deputies to examine this bill is decidely against it. Few Legislative measures have ever given rise to so much recrimination and hostility. Competition is certainly useful, and consequently moderate competition should be admitted. Colonial Sutrar has a great advantage in being cheap, for after having paid its freight, and acquitted its import duty, amounting to 100 per cent, on its value in the colonies, it it still able to stand its ground against the competition of Beetroot Sugar Consequently colonial Sugar should be supported. But who can say to what extent improvement in the manufacturing of Beetroot Sugar may be carried, and if it will not one day be produced at as cheap a rate as colonial Su«ar ? This is possible Besides, should war break out, and France be deprived of her colonies, it must be owned that it is not easy to make a choice between two subjects of such vast importance. It is absurd to say that the consumption of Sugar is n»t so great as the produce, for consumption will increase, and besides, we must not forget that the inhabitants of our colonies are Frenchmen, and deserve our utmost solicitude. The native manufacturers have also a right to the protection of Government, for it is impossible to destroy tbat branch of Industry, after having given so much encouragement.

A conciliatory system must, therefore, be adopted- 1. The entrance duties on colonial Sugar should be modified, so that the advantages ot the two Sugars should be equal. 2. The extra duty on foreign Sugar should alto be modified. 3. The manufacture of Beetroot Sugar should also be preserved, on account of its being highiy useful to tha agricultural interest.

THE EAST QUESTION. (Correspondent of the Toulonnais ) Vouula Bay, Dkc 31, 1839. The eastern question continues to absorb public aitentioii, through the question is one winch principally concerns sea ports. It is evident that the contest existing between Turkey and the Pacha of Egypt can but little ailed the tranquillity of Europe, which will always be able to prevent its causing a universal war, and becoming what is usually called a European question. No long as the Russians shall he masters of the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles watched by the combined fleet of France and England, there is but little danger that the ambition of the Pacha of Egypt will succeed in disturbing the peace of the world ; but beyond this circumscribed horizon, there exist immense interests which admit of no conciliation. England and Rus-

sia are secretly struggling for supremacy in Asia. This is the real eastern question, and it mav with truth be called the Anglo-Russian question, for the sole matter in discussion is, which of the two powers shall possess the trade of the east, and what measures shall be employed to attain that purpose? Placed as we are to examint the question, we sre of opinion that the mission of M de Brunow, in London, is a mere trick to delay the salulion of peace between the Pacha and the Sultan, and a snare intended to entrap French diplomacy. On the one hand, thi» mission, in our eyes, appears to be intended to frighten us by the idea of being isolated ; and, on the otuer hand, the warm manner in which Lord Palmerston has received the Russian envoy, appears to be a kind of invitation for us to connect ourselves more closely with the policy of England. It is as has been said, that if Russia succeeded in gaining over England to concur in making a division, which is impracticable, France would be obliged to sheath her sword aud await a fit opportunity for taking her revenge for having been so cruelly deceived. þÿ We sitall endeavour to explain why it is impossible for England and Russia to agree on a question which can sutler no arrangement between two powers that have such opposite interests. What does England want? She wants to preserve her Indian possessions, to secure Asia, and especially Egypt, which she would like to make a point ot junction for her commercial communication between Europe and

India. What does Russia covet? The trade of the east or of Asia, aud to turn to account her possession of the Black Saa, which, without that trade, can be of littf use to her. The wants of Englaud are apparent þÿ When steam shall have accomplished its commercial revolution, the navigation of the ocean will cease to be practicable, on account of there being no means of supplying steamers with coal ; and. consequently, owing to the immense distance by sea between London and Calcutta, the rich produce of India must be brought to Europe as it was during the prosperity ofVetiice. and this renders it absolutely necessary for England to possess Egypt. Russia, after having subjugated the coasts of the Biack Sea. is desirous of possessing Constantinople and the Dardanelles, in order to find a market tor the produce of her new conquests. Trebisond would make a good port of transit, and Constantinople a genera) depdt. But what would become of the two ports if Englaud was to become mistress of Egypt? Alexandria would eclipse Constantinople. The trade of the east cannot have two such roads Beside, Egypt would be the shorter and the safe road, and the continental one would become a burden for Russia. The question presented in this light ceases to be obscure In two words, the east is a store of wealth, and England and Russia are struggling for the possession. Here there can lie no division. Russia and England, though still at great distances from each other, sre manifestly in a state of rivslship. What

would be their feelings if their possessions were adjoining þÿ that is to say, if one were to be at Alexandria and the other at Constantinople ? Russia offering to give up the treaty of Unkiar Skelessy on condition of occupying

BAW33C Asia Minor, is evidently seeking her own interest. What would be the use of possessing Constantinople if an enemy existed on the Asi atic side ? The conquest of Constantinopie requires the possession of Asia Minor, and if France and England allowed themselves to be caught in so flagrant a manner, their fleets would not be able to pass the Dardanelles. and Constantinople would, in spite of Austria, become the prey of Russia. So long as this power shall not possess Asia Minor, she will manifest "no desire of laying hold of Constantinople. If you wish peace to last some time longer, Russia must not be permitted to set Iter foot in Asia Minor. A war is inevitable between Russia and England sooner or later, and will last till one of the two powers shall have in a measure disappeared. What does France want? It must be to conciliate Egypt and Turkey, to prevent a war disastrous to Europe, to await tranquiliy till hostilities shall become inevitable between England and Russia, or to delay, as much as possible, the commencement of that awful event ! I þÿ to equip as many ships as she can, so at to be ready to effect a powerful diversion as an ally, or to tight on her own account ! ! When war shall have broken forth, what will France do then ? England will be fighting for the possession of Egpyt, which France cannot allow þÿ Russia lor Constantinople, and France cannot allow that either. What a Strang# perplexity ! We cannot destroy the Russian navy, for we arc the allies of secondary maritime powers. We

can ne titer possess Constantinople, nor European Turkey ; and Kossia would, undoubtedly, retort upon us severely in Europe, which would be excessively agreeable to our national pride Russia would sooner see us in possession of Egypt than England, because without India, Egypt would t>e a mere colony, incapable of injuring tne commercial greatness of Constantinople. What would England give us ? She cannot give us Constantinople. nor þÿEgypt still less Malta, Corfu, Gibraltar; site might, perhaps, give us the Balearic Islands. The English aristocracy must regret at present having deprived us of Belgium in 1815; for if we possessed it, Russia would have nothing to offer us The treaties of 1815 are the point of a dagger turned towards the heart of England In a word, the Euglislt alliance is good, so long as war shall not brem out in the east. The Russian alliance is imperative, as soon as that event shall take place.

We have received the following important letter hoin our correspondent in Aiexundna. it will be seen Uiat ..iencuiol All is preparing lor ueieiice at ail points ALEXANDRIA, Jan. 19. Affairs have, since my last, assumed a very serious aspect, and every tlnng notv proclaims us to be upon the eve ol a war, which 1 fear will be more suiious tbati is generally imagined ; lor it cannot be supposed that the i'aeha of Egypt would dare, unless backed by some powertul ally, to oppose by force the wishes ol any one ot the European nations, and yet he is now making every possible exertion to try Ins strength against

ATI'S Russia, Austria, and England, arid this while crippled, by being obliged to keep the whole of his army in Syria to prevent the Syrians from rising against his authority on exhausted treasury, and his own country reduced to the lowest state of wretchedness. Notwithstanding all this, his Highness has positively refused to give up the Turkish fleet, although menaced by our Consul General " with a blockade of his own ports, or even worse, and to whom lie replied, that unless the blockading fleet was a very strong one, he should himself take command of the Turkish and Egyptian fleets, and bent us! ! What do you think of this? He has really been so much flattered that lie positively believes hiinsell to ho the Colossus he wishes to lie.

Every one here, especially the merchants are in a state of great uneasiness, for it is also reported that Austria is to send a land arinv to eo operate with our fleet. The Pacha alone keeps up his spirits and his resolution. He is making enormous efforts to raise a military force for the protection of Egvpt, w ithout withdrawing any of his troops from Syria ; he has already armed, and is training, the workmen of the arsenal arid dock yard ; lie has also commenced levying two regiments of 4000 men each, of militia, from among the townspeople and shopkeepers, and has given high military rank to several ol the merchants >Se\ d Mahomed el-Ghathi, a Mogrebin, and the richest of the native merchants, has been made a General Rev, and is to have command ot the militia, and Mahomed Ecdrcddiii is made a Colonel Bey, and these worthies have promised to raise this force of 8000 men in a lew days, and have already succeeded tolerably well. þÿ Mehemet Ali expect, in a few days, to have in Alexandria an army of 120,000 men, independent of his army in Sytia. A camp of 40,000 men is to be formed in the Delta, and a corps of reserve to be placed in Caito ; indeed, it is this day reported that a militia force is to be raised in that city, the command of which is to be given to the Sheiks. This I cannot vouch for, but shall be able, 1 hope, to let you know before 1 close. The Pacha is extremely active ; he is everv dav afloat, and visits one or two vessels daily, and remains on board to superintend them

while at exercise. The vessel are manned by an equal number of Tutks and Arabs ; it is reported that he got this hint from .Marshal Moult. Let it, however, come from whatever quarter it mav, it is certainly good advice ; for the crews of the Sultan's fleet are not quite as satisfied with their present berths as a they ought to be, and would gladly avail themselves of the first opportunity to return to Constantinople. The Pacha lias signified to our Consul General that th litst appearance of our fleet will be t he signal for him to close his ports ; riot a vessel, letter, parcel, or passenger, shall be allowed egress or ingress. This, of course, would he the result and object of the blockade, which he appears to have forgotten ; but long-continued hostilities would be the ruin of every mercantile house here, and would also be vary injurious to the ovarium! communication with India, tin additional reason for the speedy adjustment of affairs. þÿ Ought we not to have a force in the Red Sea sullicient to ensure communication with India in case of need ( A lew of the Hon Compa- U
ny vessels of war, and one or two steamers, ' would ensure us aid from India in case of necessity, and would awe many of the Arab tribes from rendering even iorced assistance to the Pacha.,

Improvement in tiir Str.vm Engine, þÿ A gentleman of this town informs us, that he has invented a new engine, immensely superior in every respect to the old steam engine. þÿ The power is created by air and steam. It wil consume only one half the quantity of fuel of the old one ; and the rapidity bv which a vessel propelled by it will sail will enable it to perform a passage to America in six days. Owing to a particular way in which the power acts upon the vessel, twenty miles the hour can be realized with the greatest possible ease. The weight of machinery will be only one-half that required by the oid steam engine, and instead of straining and weakening the ship, will brace and strengthen it. By this method the steam power is more than doubled. þÿ Liverpool paper.
